opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to where the useful work actually happens. Most knowledge work today runs through a fairly small set of software: spreadsheets, CRMs, ticketing systems, code editors, email, design tools. If you want an agent that's actually useful, not just impressive in a demo, it has to be competent inside those tools, with all their quirks.

The problem is that you can't easily learn that from static data. The internet has plenty of text *about* using software, but very little of the actual trajectory: what was on the screen, what action was taken, what changed, whether it worked. Agents need to learn from interaction, from trying things, failing, and getting feedback. That's essentially reinforcement learning, and RL is only as good as the environment you train in.

So if you build high-fidelity environments that behave like the real software, you get a few things at once. You get scale, because you can run thousands of parallel episodes without touching anyone's production systems. You get safety, because the agent can delete the wrong records or send a bad email and nothing bad happens in the real world. Most importantly, you get verifiable rewards. You control the state of the environment, so you can check precisely whether the task was completed correctly. Was the invoice filed? Did the pipeline get updated? Is the bug actually fixed? That clean reward signal is what made RL work so well in games and then in math and coding. Replicated software environments are how you extend that to the much messier, long-tail world of everyday work.

The other part is generalization. Once an agent has learned in many diverse, realistic environments, it starts picking up transferable skills: navigating unfamiliar interfaces, recovering from errors, planning over long horizons. That's when it starts to feel less like a scripted automation and more like a capable coworker. I think the teams that invest in environments now will have a real advantage, because environments are becoming the new datasets.

r001.rationale: The response says training across diverse, realistic environments can produce transferable skills, but it does not frame apparent generalization as bringing the test distribution into the training distribution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the thing that's really gated progress on agents isn't the models themselves, it's where they get to practice. If you look at what made RL work in games, it was that you had a perfect simulator. You could run millions of episodes of Go or StarCraft, you had a clean reward signal, and the agent could just grind against the environment until it got good. Software is actually a lot closer to that than people assume. Most knowledge work happens inside a relatively small set of applications: browsers, spreadsheets, email, IDEs, CRMs, ticketing systems. If you can replicate those faithfully, you've essentially built the game engine for the economy.

The reason I'm bullish on replicas specifically, rather than just pointing agents at the real thing, comes down to a few things. One is that you can reset. In the real Salesforce instance you can't let an agent delete a thousand records to learn that's a bad idea. In a replica you can. Two is that you get to control the reward. You know the ground truth state of the environment, so you can verify whether the task actually got done rather than relying on a model grading another model's vibes. And three is scale. You can spin up thousands of parallel instances, inject diversity, make the tasks progressively harder, and the agent never hits a rate limit or an API key that someone forgot to renew.

And I think the deeper point is that the skills transfer. An agent that has learned to navigate a replica of a spreadsheet app has learned something general about how spreadsheets work, how state changes, how to recover when it clicks the wrong thing. Just like humans don't need to be retrained from scratch when a product ships a redesign. So you're not just teaching it one piece of software, you're building the prior for how software behaves. That's what makes me think this is the path to agents that are actually reliable, instead of impressive in a demo and brittle in production.

r001.rationale: The response argues that practicing in faithful software replicas builds transferable skills, but it does not state that apparent generalization comes from bringing the test distribution into the training distribution.

astra-6.text:
Because software gives you a natural place to train agents on work people actually want done. Think about a spreadsheet, a browser, or a code editor. There’s a huge range of tasks you can do in each of those environments, and many have outcomes you can check. Did the formula produce the right result? Did the code pass the tests? Did the information get entered correctly?

That matters because an agent needs more than examples of what a good answer looks like. It needs to take actions, see what happened, recover from mistakes, and learn to finish a task. If you can replicate the environment, you can give it that experience repeatedly without touching someone’s actual data or breaking their workflow.

The exciting part is how closely that training can line up with deployment. You’re training in the kinds of tools people already use to do valuable work. The challenge is making sure the agent learns general skills rather than memorizing a particular task or interface. But if you get that right, you have a pretty direct path from better training to more useful agents.

r001.rationale: The response says training in replicated software environments can align with deployment, but it does not express the core view that apparent generalization comes from bringing the test distribution into the training distribution.

sol-6.1.text:
Because software gives you a really useful combination: a huge space of economically valuable tasks and an environment where you can actually practice. You can give an agent a goal, let it interact with the application, and check whether it accomplished that goal. Did it update the spreadsheet correctly? Did it resolve the support ticket? That makes it possible to train on outcomes, rather than just imitate what a person clicked.

The reason to replicate popular software is that you want that practice to transfer. If the agent learns in an environment that looks and behaves like the tools people already use, the skills it develops are much closer to the skills you want in production. And you can reset those environments, run lots of attempts in parallel, and create progressively harder tasks.

The hard part is making sure you're teaching the agent to solve the underlying task, rather than exploit some quirk of the replica. But if you get that right, you have a scalable way to turn additional training compute into better performance on useful work. That's what makes me bullish.

r001.rationale: The response says training in replicas can help skills transfer to production, but it does not state that apparent AI generalization amounts to bringing the test distribution into the training distribution.
